text: Instruction tuning trains on instruction-response pairs, but a model only ever sees a flat sequence of tokens — there's no native concept of whose turn it is. Something has to turn a structured conversation into that flat sequence, consistently, every time. That's a chat template.

ChatML is one widely used style: every turn gets wrapped in explicit role markers, like im-start-system or im-start-assistant, closed with im-end. Those markers are special tokens added to the vocabulary specifically for this purpose — they never show up as ordinary text, which is what lets code reliably detect exactly where a turn starts and ends.

The correct way to build this is never to hand-concatenate strings yourself. Hugging Face tokenizers store the model's exact chat template, often as a Jinja2 template bundled with the tokenizer config, and expose it through apply_chat_template, which takes a list of role and content dicts and produces the correctly formatted sequence — including, when you ask for it, the marker that signals it's now the assistant's turn to generate.

Here's why this matters so much: the single most damaging SFT mistake is training on one format and serving at inference with a slightly different one — different whitespace, a missing newline. The model learned to associate specific patterns with "a turn just started," so even a small mismatch degrades quality silently, with no error thrown.

The fix is procedural: build both your training data and your inference prompts through the same apply_chat_template call, from the same tokenizer. Up next: formatting is solved, so where does the instruction-response data itself actually come from?
